title: Mousse au Chocolat
subtitle: Classic French dark chocolate mousse
excerpt: Dark chocolate melted and combined with egg yolks and folded with whipped egg whites into a light, airy mousse. The most widely made of all French chocolate desserts, and one of the easiest to get exactly right.
sourceNotes: Mousse au chocolat is a 20th-century creation, the first recipes appear in French cookbooks from the early 1900s, after chocolate became widely available in France. Julia Child, Mastering the Art of French Cooking (1961), gives the authoritative method, establishing the ratio of chocolate to eggs. Elizabeth David includes the recipe in her later works. The classic version contains no cream, the airy texture comes entirely from the whipped egg whites.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Must be made at least 2 hours ahead. Keeps in the fridge for up to 3 days, covered. The texture firms slightly over time.

glossaryTerms.definition: The technique of gently combining a lighter mixture (whipped egg whites or cream) into a heavier one (chocolate) without deflating the air that has been incorporated. Use a large rubber spatula in a cutting and turning motion rather than stirring. The aim is to combine the mixtures with the minimum number of strokes — over-folding produces a dense, flat mousse.

content.text: Mousse au chocolat is one of the most forgiving of the French classic desserts. It has three components, melted chocolate, egg yolks, whipped egg whites, and one critical technique:
the whites into the chocolate base without losing the air you have worked to put in them. Done well, the mousse is airy but rich; done poorly, it is still a very good chocolate dessert.

Melt the chocolate and butter together in a heatproof bowl set over barely simmering water (bain-marie), stirring until smooth. Remove from the heat and allow to cool for 5 minutes, it should be warm but not hot.
Stir the egg yolks into the chocolate one at a time, mixing well after each. Add the salt. Set aside.
Whisk the egg whites to soft peaks with the electric mixer. Add the sugar and whisk to stiff, glossy peaks. The whites should hold their shape but not look dry.

Add a large spoonful of the egg white to the chocolate mixture and stir vigorously to loosen it. Then add the remaining egg white in two or three additions, folding gently with a large spatula. Use a cutting and turning motion, do not stir. Stop as soon as no white streaks remain.
Divide among glasses or ramekins. Refrigerate for at least 2 hours. Serve cold.

items.symptom: The mousse is dense rather than airy
items.cause: The egg whites were under-whipped, or the chocolate base was too hot when the whites were folded in, partially cooking and deflating them.
items.fix: Whisk the whites to stiff but not dry peaks. Allow the chocolate to cool until just warm (body temperature) before folding. Over-mixing also deflates the mousse, stop as soon as the whites are incorporated.

items.symptom: The mousse has set with visible streaks of white
items.cause: The whites were not fully folded in.
items.fix: A few extra folds would have resolved this. A couple of white streaks will not affect the flavour but do indicate slightly under-mixed mousse.

items.cause: The chocolate seized, contact with a small amount of water caused it to clump.
items.fix: Ensure all utensils are completely dry when melting chocolate. Even a single drop of water can cause chocolate to seize. If it has seized, try adding a tablespoon of warm cream and stirring vigorously to rescue it.

content.text: Mousse au chocolat has been on French tables since the early 20th century. It is the standard home dessert for dinner parties and birthdays across France. Four ingredients, one technique. The cream-free version is the older style: darker and more intense than the cream versions that spread in the 1970s.
